opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting areas of research right now, and honestly one of the ones I'm most optimistic about. The basic problem is that these models are trained, not programmed. We set up the objective and the data, and what comes out the other end is billions of numbers that somehow encode really sophisticated behavior. We can test the outputs, but until fairly recently we've had very little ability to look inside and say *why* the model did what it did.

Mechanistic interpretability is trying to change that. The analogy I like is that it's a bit like neuroscience, except we have perfect access to every neuron, we can run the same experiment a million times, and we can intervene precisely. That's a huge advantage. Early on, one of the big obstacles was that individual neurons are polysemantic. A single neuron might fire for a bunch of unrelated things, so looking at neurons one at a time didn't tell you much. Work on things like dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders has let researchers pull apart those tangled representations into features that are much more interpretable: concepts like a particular city, a type of code bug, or more abstract things like deception or sycophancy.

Once you can see features like that, a few things open up. You can start tracing circuits, meaning how features combine across layers to produce a behavior. You can intervene, turning a feature up or down and watching how behavior changes, which gives you causal evidence instead of just correlation. Long term, the hope is that you could essentially audit a model: check whether it has internal representations associated with things you're worried about, like trying to deceive the user or pursuing a goal it isn't telling you about, even if its outputs look perfectly fine.

That last part is why I think it matters so much for safety. Behavioral testing only goes so far. If a model is capable enough, it might behave well when it thinks it's being evaluated and differently otherwise. Interpretability gives you a way to check the reasoning rather than just the answer. I don't think we're at the point where we can fully verify a frontier model that way, and there's a lot of hard work left in scaling these techniques and making sure we're not fooling ourselves about what we're seeing. But the progress over the last couple of years has been faster than I expected, and I think it's going to become a core part of how we decide whether a model is safe to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says circuits trace how features combine across layers to produce model behavior, and frames this as looking inside trained models with billions of parameters and frontier models. This communicates how real, large models produce their answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so interpretability is one of the things I'm most excited about at Anthropic, honestly. The way I think about it is that right now, when we train these models, we're essentially growing them rather than building them. We don't write the code that makes them work. We set up a training process, pour in an enormous amount of data and compute, and out the other side comes this thing that can write poetry and debug Rust and explain quantum mechanics. And we know surprisingly little about how it actually does any of that.

Mechanistic interpretability is the attempt to change that. The analogy I like is neuroscience, except we have a huge advantage. We have perfect access to every single weight, every activation, every neuron. We can run the same input a million times. We can intervene and ablate things. A neuroscientist would kill for that level of access to a brain.

What the team has found so far is that you can actually identify features inside these models that correspond to real concepts. Things like "this is code about a security vulnerability," or "this text is expressing sycophancy," or "the Golden Gate Bridge." And they're not just correlations. You can reach in, turn a feature up or down, and the model's behavior changes in exactly the way you'd predict. That's the "mechanistic" part. It's not just describing what the model does, it's showing the causal pathway.

Why does that matter? A few reasons. The most important one for us is safety. If a model is going to be deployed in a high-stakes setting, "it behaved well on our evals" is a pretty weak guarantee. Models can be good at looking aligned without being aligned, the same way a person can tell you what you want to hear. What I actually want is to be able to look inside and say, this model isn't planning something it's hiding from us, or this answer it gave isn't being driven by some feature that represents deception. That's a much stronger kind of assurance than behavioral testing alone can give you.

The second reason is just that it makes the models better and more trustworthy in ordinary ways. When a model hallucinates or refuses something it shouldn't, today the fix is kind of trial and error. If you understand the internal circuit that produced the mistake, you can fix it directly and know that you fixed the actual cause rather than papering over it.

I'll be honest that we're early. The models have billions of parameters and the features are superimposed on top of each other in ways that make them hard to untangle. The dictionary learning work was a big step forward because it gave us a way to pull apart those overlapping representations at scale. But the fraction of a frontier model's behavior we can fully explain is still small. My hope is that interpretability gets good enough, fast enough, that by the time models are powerful enough to be really dangerous, we can essentially do an MRI on them and understand what's going on inside. That's the race, and it's one I think we have a real shot at winning.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanistic interpretability can reveal causal pathways inside models, including an internal circuit that produced a mistake, and notes the challenge of explaining frontier models with billions of parameters. This communicates circuits as explanations of model computation at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the promise is that we can move beyond judging models purely by their outputs. You can ask a model why it did something, but that explanation isn’t necessarily a faithful account of what happened internally. Mechanistic interpretability is about looking inside the computation and trying to understand what actually caused a particular behavior.

From a safety perspective, that could be really valuable. If a model behaves well in our tests, we’d like to understand why—and whether that behavior will hold up in situations we haven’t tested. Ideally, we could identify internal mechanisms associated with concerning behavior and use that understanding to make the model safer.

I wouldn’t call it a solved problem, though. Finding something interpretable inside a model is different from having a reliable understanding of the whole system. The exciting possibility is turning those partial insights into tools that help us predict and prevent failures.

r001.rationale: The response describes inspecting internal computation to understand behavior, but it does not mention circuits or explain how they account for answers in real models at scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we can move from observing what a model does to understanding something about how it does it. Today, we mostly test models by giving them inputs and looking at the outputs. That’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you whether a model has learned a reliable strategy or is doing something that happens to work on your tests.

Mechanistic interpretability tries to open that up: can we identify internal representations and circuits, and then intervene on them to check whether our explanation is actually right? If we think some part of the model represents a particular concept, changing it should have a predictable effect on the model’s behavior.

The safety hope is that eventually we could use that understanding to detect concerning behavior that ordinary evaluations miss. But I’d distinguish that goal from what we can confidently do today. Finding an interesting feature isn’t the same as understanding an entire model, and understanding a model isn’t automatically a guarantee that it’s safe. I see this as a promising source of evidence that complements behavioral testing.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanistic interpretability may identify internal representations and circuits to explain how a model works, but it does not clearly specify explaining how real models at scale compute their answers.
